## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

This reference covers a subset of the Cucumber documentation: the BDD section and the Gherkin section, every page of each, all read in full. Nothing here describes pages outside the subset. Where a taken page links to a page outside it (step definitions, the API reference on tags and hooks, the anti-patterns guide, the user-story glossary entry, blog posts), this reference records the link and not the linked content. The source is the Cucumber tool's product documentation. It reports no studies, measurements or data, and its recommendations, rules of thumb and historical account are the documentation's practitioner assertions, not demonstrated findings; the `[AP]` and `[AR]` markers below mark them as the documentation's own claims.

The BDD section presents Behaviour-Driven Development as "the software development process that Cucumber was built to support", and adds: "There's much more to BDD than just using Cucumber." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Behaviour-Driven Development"). BDD is a way for software teams to work that "closes the gap between business people and technical people" [V] by encouraging collaboration across roles to build shared understanding of the problem, working in rapid, small iterations to increase feedback and the flow of value, and producing system documentation that is automatically checked against the system's behaviour [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?"). The means is a focus on concrete, real-world examples of how the system should behave, used to guide the work from concept to implementation [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?"). BDD does not replace an existing agile process; the documentation calls it "a set of plugins for your existing process" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "BDD and agile").

The day-to-day work is a three-step, iterative process the documentation names *Discovery*, *Formulation* and *Automation*: talk about concrete examples of a small upcoming change, document them in a form that can be automated, then implement each documented example starting from an automated test [AR] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"). The documentation holds that the order matters. It treats the tests and documentation as side-effects of the real goal, valuable working software, which it says is reached fastest through conversations between the people who imagine and deliver it [AR] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Discovery: What it _could_ do"); it tells newcomers to start with discovery, and its myths page says that formulating scenarios before effective discovery is "a waste of time" and that automating scenarios after the code is written is test automation, "but it's not BDD" [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can pick and choose the practices in any order"; "Myth: You can automate scenarios after the code is implemented").

Gherkin is the medium for formulation: "a medium that can be read by both humans and computers" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Formulation: What it _should_ do"). The writing guidance in both sections makes four recurring points: scenarios describe behaviour, not implementation; examples are concrete and make no assumptions about technology; the same thing is said the same way every time; and outcomes are checked on observable output, with implementation details kept in step definitions [AR] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour"; docs/bdd/examples.md, "Examples"; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios"; docs/gherkin/reference.md, "When"; "Then"). The Gherkin reference specifies the keywords, step arguments and localisation, and the step-organization page advises grouping step definitions by domain concept and pushing reuse into helper methods [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference"; docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Grouping step definitions").

## Part I: Behaviour-Driven Development (the BDD section)

### What BDD is

The landing page describes how BDD works:

> "We do this by focusing collaborative work around concrete, real-world examples that illustrate how we want the system to behave. We use those examples to guide us from concept through to implementation, in a process of continuous collaboration."
> (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?")

**BDD and agile.** The page assumes the team already uses some kind of agile methodology, planning work in small increments of value such as User Stories [AP]. "BDD does not replace your existing agile process, it enhances it." [V] It describes BDD as plugins that make the team more able to deliver on the promises of agile, which it lists as timely, reliable releases of working software that meets the organisation's evolving needs; the sentence ends with the phrase "requiring some maintenance effort and discipline" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "BDD and agile").

**Rapid iterations.** The page assumes the reader wants to respond quickly to user feedback and do only the minimal work needed to meet those needs [AP]. BDD encourages working in rapid iterations, "continuously breaking down your user's problems into small pieces that can flow through your development process as quickly as possible" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Rapid iterations").

### Three practices

Day-to-day BDD activity is described as "a three-step, iterative process" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"):

1. Take a small upcoming change to the system (a User Story) and talk about concrete examples of the new functionality to explore, discover and agree on the details of what is expected [AP].
2. Document those examples in a way that can be automated, and check for agreement [AP].
3. Implement the behaviour each documented example describes, starting with an automated test to guide the development of the code [AP].

Each change is kept small and iterated rapidly, "moving back up a level each time you need more information" [V]. Each newly automated and implemented example adds something valuable to the system and leaves the team ready to respond to feedback [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"). The three practices are named Discovery, Formulation and Automation [AP], and the page's figure, alt text "Diagram of how the practices fit together", carries the caption "Discovery, Formulation and Automation" (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"). The tape carries the alt text and caption only.

The page then states what the documented examples become over time:

> "Over time, the documented examples become an asset that enables your team to continue confidently and rapidly making changes to the system. The code reflects the documentation, and the documentation reflects the team's shared understanding of the problem domain. This shared understanding is constantly evolving."
> (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices")

#### Discovery: what it *could* do

The section opens with an epigraph from Fred Brooks, *The mythical man-month*: "The hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build." [V] [BT] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Discovery: What it _could_ do").

The page argues that although a BDD team produces documentation and automated tests, these can be thought of as "nice side-effects" [V]; the real goal is valuable, working software, and the fastest way there is through conversations between the people involved in imagining and delivering it [AR] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Discovery: What it _could_ do"). BDD helps teams have the right conversations at the right time, so that time in meetings is minimised and valuable code is maximised [AP]. The conversations are structured ones called discovery workshops, focused on real-world examples of the system from the users' perspective; they grow the team's shared understanding of users' needs, of the rules that govern how the system should function, and of the scope of what needs to be done [AP]. "It may also reveal gaps in our understanding, where we need more information before we know what to do." [V] The scrutiny of a discovery session "often reveals low-priority functionality that can be deferred from the scope of a user story" [V], helping the team work in smaller increments and improving flow [AP].

For newcomers: "If you're new to BDD, discovery is the right place to start. You won't get much joy from the other two practices until you've mastered discovery." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Discovery: What it _could_ do").

#### Formulation: what it *should* do

Once the team has at least one valuable example from discovery, it formulates each example as structured documentation, which the page says gives a quick way to confirm the team really does share an understanding of what to build [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Formulation: What it _should_ do"). In contrast to traditional documentation, BDD uses "a medium that can be read by both humans and computers" [V] (the phrase links to the Gherkin section), so that the whole team can give feedback on the shared vision and the examples can later be automated to guide development [AP]. Writing this executable specification collaboratively establishes a shared language for talking about the system, which "helps us to use problem-domain terminology all the way down into the code" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Formulation: What it _should_ do").

#### Automation: what it *actually does*

With the executable specification in hand, the team takes one example at a time and automates it by connecting it to the system as a test. The test fails because the behaviour is not implemented yet; the team then develops the implementation code, guided as required by lower-level examples of the behaviour of internal system components [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_"). That phrase links to an article at geepawhill.org whose URL slug is `microtest-tdd-more-definition` [BT].

"The automated examples work like guide-rails, helping us to keep our development work on track." [V] When the system is maintained later, the automated examples help the team understand what the system currently does and make changes safely without unintentionally breaking anything [AP]. "This rapid, repeatable feedback reduces the burden of manual regression testing, freeing people up to do more interesting work, like exploratory testing." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_").

The page closes with "Learn more", a single sentence pointing to "the topics below" [AP]; the tape carries no list after it, only three link definitions (docs/bdd/index.md, "Learn more").

### Who does what?

The page asks who should write Gherkin documents and who should write step definitions, noting that product owners, business analysts, programmers and testers are often confused about who takes on which responsibilities [AP]. It says the answer depends on several factors, such as team structure, skills, culture and process [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Who does what?").

#### The Three Amigos

The Three Amigos is "a meeting that takes user stories and turns them into clean, thorough Gherkin scenarios" [V], involving "three voices (at least)" [V] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos"):

- **The product owner** is most concerned with the scope of the application, which involves translating user stories into a series of features; as the tester raises edge cases, the product owner decides what is within scope [AP].
- **The tester** generates lots of Scenarios and lots of edge cases, asking how the application will break and which user stories the Features have not accounted for [AP].
- **The developer** adds many of the Steps to the Scenarios and thinks of the details that go into each requirement, asking how the application will execute and what roadblocks or requirements sit behind the scenes [AP].

The page's argument: these conversations can produce great tests because each amigo sees the product from a different perspective, and for this reason it is essential that all of these roles discover examples together [AR] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos"). It names Example Mapping and Event Storming as "great collaborative analysis techniques for discovering examples" [V]. It adds that "there is no reason to limit these meetings to three people—or to hold only one such meeting at the beginning of the project" [V], and advises continually refining features and collaborating with everyone [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos").

#### Writing Gherkin

At the start, while the language and style of the scenarios is still being established, "it is recommended that the entire team collaborate on writing the Gherkin" [V]. Later it can be done efficiently by a pair, a developer (or whoever is responsible for the automation) and a tester (or whoever is responsible for quality), as long as the product owner (or business representative) actively reviews their output [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing Gherkin").

#### Writing features

Cucumber tests are written in terms of Features, each consisting of one or more Scenarios [AP]. The page's example Feature file, "Explaining Cucumber", has the lines "In order to gain an understanding of the Cucumber testing system", "As a non-programmer" and "I want to have an overview of Cucumber that is understandable by non-geeks", and one scenario, "A worker seeks an overview of Cucumber", in which a coworker explains Cucumber [AE] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing features"). The page points out that the scenario does not go into the details of what the software (here, the coworker) will do; it stays with the perspective of the person the Feature serves [AP].

Every feature file has a single feature description at the top and any number of scenarios [AP]. The `Feature` line names the feature and should be a short label. `In order to` gives the reason or justification for the feature and should generally match one of the project's core purposes or business values; the page lists protect revenue, increase revenue, manage cost, increase brand value, make the product remarkable, and provide more value to your customers [AP]. `As a` describes the role of the people or users the feature serves, and `I want` is a one-sentence explanation of what the Feature is expected to do [AP]. "So, those three lines cover Why, Who, and What." [V] The scenarios then supply the "How" [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing features").

#### Scenarios

A feature may have any number of scenarios, but lots and lots of them may mean the document describes more than one feature, in which case the page recommends splitting it; it calls the threshold subjective and leaves the call to the reader [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios"). A scenario's first line briefly describes what it covers: "If you can’t describe your scenario in a single sentence (and not a run-on sentence), then it’s probably trying to cover too much" [V], and it should be split [AP].

Steps begin with `Given`, `When` and `Then` "(typically in that order)" [V]; repeated keywords can be replaced with `And` or `But` for readability [AP]. Any `Given` step line should generally describe only one thing; a word like "and" in the middle of a step suggests more than one step, which should be split [AP]. The page's worked example splits a `When` step that fills in both a "Name" and an "Address" field into two steps [AE] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios").

"Cucumber features are best served by consistency." [V] The page's example: `Given I am logged in` and `Given I have logged in to the site` mean the same thing, so the team should pick one and use the same line in every scenario that needs it [AE] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios").

### Discovery workshop

A discovery workshop is "a conversation where technical and business people collaborate to explore, discover and agree as much as they can about the desired behaviour" [V] for a User Story (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "What is a discovery workshop?").

The page lists three of "several" workshop models, calling them "just a few" [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "How do you conduct a discovery workshop?"):

- **Example Mapping** uses index cards in four colours to map rules (a summary of the constraints or acceptance criteria the team has agreed) to examples (illustrations or cases of those criteria) [AP].
- **OOPSI Mapping (Outcomes, Outputs, Processes, Scenarios, Inputs)**, linked to a page at jennyjmar.com, is similar to Example Mapping and uses Post-it Notes of different colours to map shared processes and relationships between outputs and scenarios [AP] [BT].
- **Feature Mapping**, linked to a page at johnfergusonsmart.com, also uses coloured Post-it Notes: the team picks a story from the backlog, identifies the actors, breaks the story into tasks, and maps those tasks to specific examples [AP] [BT].

**When.** "As late as possible before development on a new User Story begins, in order to prevent details from being lost." [V] Holding it late also leaves the team room to shift plans if new details surface [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "When should you hold a discovery workshop?").

**Who.** "A good rule-of-thumb is 3-6 people" [V], with at minimum the Three Amigos present: a product owner, who identifies the problem to solve; a developer, who addresses how to build a solution; and a tester, who addresses edge cases [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "Who should attend?").

**How long.** "A discovery workshop should ideally only last about 25-30 minutes per story." [V] Needing more time suggests the story is too large and should be broken down, or that specifics are missing, in which case the story is set aside for more research [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "How long does a discovery workshop take?").

**Why.** The purpose is to give all stakeholders, technical and non-technical, a shared understanding of the work; the page says this encourages cross-functional collaboration and more feedback, and covers lost details and incorrect assumptions [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "Why bother?"). Its conclusion calls the workshop "a very important piece of the BDD lifecycle, among other agile development approaches" and warns: "Without it, you are sure to run into miscommunications and your team won't discover any unknowns, which could really hamper your project's success." [V] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "Conclusion").

### Example Mapping

Before a user story is pulled into development, the page says a conversation to clarify and confirm its acceptance criteria is crucial, and "Example Mapping is a method designed to make this conversation short and very productive." [V] (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "Example Mapping").

Concrete examples are described as a great way to explore and understand the problem domain and a great basis for acceptance tests [AP]. Discussing examples brings up other things worth capturing: **rules** that summarise a set of examples or express other constraints; **questions** that cannot be answered in the conversation, or assumptions that are made; and new **user stories** discovered, or sliced and deferred out of scope [AP] (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works"). These go on index cards arranged in a map [AP]:

- the story on a **yellow** card, on top;
- each acceptance criterion, or rule, on a **blue** card beneath the story;
- examples illustrating each rule on **green** cards under the relevant rule;
- questions that cannot be answered in the session on **red** cards, so the conversation can move on.

The page assigns no card colour to new user stories. "We keep going until the group is satisfied that the scope of the story is clear, or we run out of time." [V] (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works"). For more, it points to Matt Wynne's blog on Example Mapping, Steve Tooke's blog on "Your first Example Mapping session", and an Example Mapping webinar, all linked under the site's `/blog/` path and outside this subset [BT] (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "More information").

### Writing better Gherkin

#### Describe behaviour

"Your scenarios should describe the intended behaviour of the system, not the implementation." [V] That is, what, not how [AP] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour"). For an authentication scenario the page recommends writing `When "Bob" logs in` instead of a five-step procedure that visits "/login", enters "Bob" and "tester" in the user name and password fields, presses the "login" button and expects the "welcome" page [AE]. It calls the first a *functional requirement* and the second a *procedural reference*: "Functional requirements are features, but procedures belong in the implementation details." [V]

The argument: when the implementation of a feature changes, only the process steps behind the scenes need to change, because "The behaviour does not have to change just because the implementation does." [V] The page offers a test question for any feature clause, "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" [V], and says that if the answer is yes, the wording should be reworked to avoid implementation-specific details; a side benefit is shorter scenarios that are easier to follow [AP] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour").

#### Consider a more declarative style

The page presents a declarative style as one way to make scenarios easier to maintain and less brittle: it describes the behaviour of the application rather than implementation details, reads better as living documentation, and "helps you focus on the value that the customer is getting, rather than the keystrokes they will use" [V] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style").

It keeps a place for the alternative: "Imperative tests communicate details, and in some contexts this style of test is appropriate." [V] But because imperative tests are closely tied to the mechanics of the current UI, "they often require more work to maintain" [V], and any change to the implementation means the tests must be updated too [AP].

The worked example is a feature, "Subscribers see different articles based on their subscription level", written twice [AE] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style"):

- **Imperative.** Each scenario types an email address and "validPassword123" into fields, presses "Submit", and checks which named articles ("FreeArticle1", "PaidArticle1") appear on the home page. The page notes that every step is a precise instruction with exact inputs and expected results, and that it is easy to imagine changes that would force the tests to change: the subscription options, or the means of logging in ("What if, in the future, users log in with a voice interface or a thumbprint?") [AE].
- **Declarative.** "Free Frieda" and "Paid Patty" have their subscriptions, log in with valid credentials, and see a Free article, or a Free and a Paid article [AE].

In the declarative version each step communicates an idea without exact values; how the user interacts with the system, which articles are free or paid, and the subscription levels of test users are specified in the step definitions, which the page glosses as the automation code that interacts with the system [AP]. The business could then change what free and paid plans include without changing this scenario or others that share its step definitions, and a new subscription level is easy to add as a scenario [AP]. Avoiding terms like "click a button" makes the scenario more resilient to UI implementation details; "The intent of the scenario remains the same, even if the implementation changes later." [V] Too many implementation details also make the intended behaviour harder to understand [AP] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style").

### Myths about BDD

The page sets out to "bust some of the most common myths and misunderstandings about BDD" [V] and names four (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myths about BDD").

**Myth: you can pick and choose the practices in any order.** The page answers with Liz Keogh's take, linked to her 2014 post on using BDD with legacy systems [BT]:

> "having conversations is more important than capturing conversations is more important than automating conversations."
> (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can pick and choose the practices in any order")

"Unless you've already done effective discovery work, trying to formulate scenarios is a waste of time." [V] Likewise, examples cannot be automated before the work of finding the most important ones to automate has been done, or before the business stakeholder has given feedback on their wording [AP] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can pick and choose the practices in any order").

**Myth: you can automate scenarios after the code is implemented.** Many people use Cucumber for test automation that checks for bugs after the code is written: "That's a perfectly reasonable way to do test automation, but it's not BDD." [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can automate scenarios after the code is implemented").

**Myth: discovery doesn't need a conversation.** The page reports, in its own voice, "We see plenty of teams" [V] that leave identifying examples and formulating scenarios to a single individual. "That's not BDD." [V] Discovery work must be collaborative, "bringing together representatives of the different specialists who all need to share understanding about what will be built" [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Discovery doesn't need a conversation").

**Myth: using Cucumber means you're doing BDD.** "Just because you're using Cucumber, doesn't mean you're doing BDD." [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Using Cucumber means you're doing BDD").

### History of BDD

The page's account, which spells the term "Behavior-driven development" [AP] (docs/bdd/history.md, "History of BDD"):

- Daniel Terhorst-North pioneered BDD in the early 2000s, as he explained in a 2006 article, "Introducing BDD" [BT]. BDD grew as a response to test-driven development (TDD), to help programmers on new agile teams "get straight to the good stuff" of knowing how to approach testing and coding, and to minimise misunderstandings [AP]. "BDD has evolved into both analysis and automated testing at the acceptance level." [V] Liz Keogh, described as another BDD pioneer, started writing and speaking about it extensively from 2004 [AP] (docs/bdd/history.md, "History of BDD").
- In 2003 Terhorst-North started writing JBehave, a replacement for JUnit using vocabulary based on "behaviour" rather than "test"; Liz Keogh and Chris Matts contributed early on [AP]. Influenced by the idea of ubiquitous language from Eric Evans' *Domain-Driven Design*, and focusing on business value, the "Given/When/Then" template "was developed to capture a story's acceptance criteria in an executable form" [V] [BT]. It grew partly from the "As a..., I ..., So that..." user-story template created by Rachel Davies at Connextra, which the page says had become a recognised standard [BT] (docs/bdd/history.md, "Early tools supporting BDD").
- In 2005 RSpec, supporting BDD in Ruby, was founded by Dave Astels, Steven Baker, Aslak Hellesøy and David Chelimsky [AP] (docs/bdd/history.md, "Early tools supporting BDD").
- **Origins of Cucumber.** While helping improve RSpec, Aslak had ideas for improvements to error messages, step definition snippets and result reporting [AP]. "RSpec was designed for programmers, whereas the RSpec Story Runner was for the whole team, including non-coding stakeholders." [V] He started a new project to make a better Story Runner, first called *Stories*; his then-fiancée suggested the name *Cucumber*, and it stuck [AP] (docs/bdd/history.md, "Origins of Cucumber").

### Examples

Good BDD examples are concrete rather than abstract: they mention names of people and places, exact dates and amounts, and anything relevant to the software's problem domain [AP]. "Good examples don't mention technical details." [V] (docs/bdd/examples.md, "Examples"). An admonition headed "Imagine it's 1922" says: "Most software does something people could do manually (just not as efficiently)." [V] It asks for examples that make no assumptions about technology: "Imagine it's 1922, when there were no computers." [V] (docs/bdd/examples.md, "Examples"). The same admonition reappears, extended, in the Gherkin reference's `When` section (see below).

## Part II: Gherkin (the Gherkin section)

### Gherkin index

The section's index page carries the heading "Gherkin" and an MDX component, `<DocCardList />`, which the tape holds as a bare tag with no text (docs/gherkin/index.mdx, "Gherkin").

### Reference: general rules

Gherkin uses a set of special keywords to give structure and meaning to executable specifications; each keyword is translated into many spoken languages, and the reference uses English [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference"). Most lines in a Gherkin document start with a keyword [AP]. Comments are allowed only at the start of a new line, anywhere in the feature file, and begin with zero or more spaces, a hash sign (`#`) and some text; "Block comments are currently not supported by Gherkin." [V] Indentation may use spaces or tabs, and two spaces is recommended [AP]. The example is a "Guess the word" feature with two scenarios, "Maker starts a game" and "Breaker joins a game" [AE] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference").

The trailing part of each step, after the keyword, is matched to a code block called a step definition [AP]. Some keywords are followed by a colon and some are not; adding a colon after one that should not have it means "your test(s) will be ignored" [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference").

### Keywords

Each non-blank line must start with a Gherkin keyword followed by any text; the only exceptions are the free-form descriptions under `Example`/`Scenario`, `Background`, `Scenario Outline` and `Rule` lines [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Keywords").

The primary keywords are `Feature`; `Rule` (as of Gherkin 6); `Example` (or `Scenario`); `Given`, `When`, `Then`, `And` and `But` for steps (or `*`); `Background`; `Scenario Outline` (or `Scenario Template`); and `Examples` (or `Scenarios`) [AP]. The secondary keywords are `"""` (Doc Strings), `|` (Data Tables), `@` (Tags) and `#` (Comments) [AP]. A note says Gherkin is localised for many spoken languages, each with its own equivalents of these keywords [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Keywords").

#### Feature

`Feature` gives a high-level description of a software feature and groups related scenarios [AP]. It must always be the first primary keyword in a Gherkin document, followed by a colon and a short text describing the feature [AP]. Free-form description text can follow underneath; Cucumber ignores those lines at runtime, but they are available for reporting, and reporting tools such as the official HTML formatter include them [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Feature"). The example describes the "Guess the word" game as turn-based for two players, a Maker and a Breaker [AE].

The name and optional description have no special meaning to Cucumber; they are a place to document important aspects of the feature, such as a brief explanation and a list of business rules (general acceptance criteria) [AP]. The description ends at the first line that starts with `Background`, `Rule`, `Example` or `Scenario Outline` (or their aliases) [AP]. Tags placed above `Feature` group related features independently of file and directory structure (the tags link points outside this subset) [AP]. A `.feature` file holds only one `Feature` [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Feature").

#### Descriptions

Free-form descriptions can also sit under `Example`/`Scenario`, `Background`, `Scenario Outline` and `Rule`: "You can write anything you like, as long as no line starts with a keyword." [V] Descriptions can be Markdown, which formatters including the official HTML formatter support [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Descriptions").

#### Rule

The optional `Rule` keyword has been part of Gherkin since v6 [AP]. It represents one *business rule* that should be implemented, provides additional information for a feature, and groups the scenarios that belong to that rule; a `Rule` should contain one or more scenarios illustrating it [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Rule"). The example, a feature called "Highlander", has the rules "There can be only One", with two examples about ninjas, and "There can be Two (in some cases)", with one example, "Two -- Dead and Reborn as Phoenix", whose steps the page elides [AE].

#### Example

An `Example` is a *concrete example* that *illustrates* a business rule and consists of a list of steps; `Scenario` is a synonym [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example"). Any number of steps is allowed, but "we recommend 3-5 steps per example" [V], and the page adds: "Having too many steps will cause the example to lose its expressive power as a specification and documentation." [V] Besides being specification and documentation, an example is also a test, and the examples as a whole are an executable specification of the system [AP]. Examples follow one pattern: an initial context (`Given`), an event (`When`), an expected outcome (`Then`) [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example").

#### Steps

Each step starts with `Given`, `When`, `Then`, `And` or `But` [AP]. Cucumber executes the steps of a scenario one at a time, in the written order, looking for a matching step definition for each [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Steps"). Keywords are not considered when matching, so no two steps may share the same text under different keywords; `Given there is money in my account` and `Then there is money in my account` count as duplicates [AE]. The page grants that "This might seem like a limitation" [V] and argues it forces a less ambiguous, clearer domain language, rewriting the pair as `Given my account has a balance of £430` and `Then my account should have a balance of £430` [AR] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Steps").

**Given.** `Given` steps describe the initial context of the system, the *scene* of the scenario, typically something that happened in the past [AP]. When Cucumber executes one, it configures the system into a well-defined state, such as creating and configuring objects or adding data to a test database [AP]. Their purpose is to put the system in a known state before the user (or an external system) starts interacting with it in the `When` steps; the page says to avoid talking about user interaction in `Given` steps, which in use-case terms would be preconditions [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Given"). Several `Given` steps are fine, with `And` or `But` from the second onwards [AP]. The examples: "Mickey and Minnie have started a game", "I am logged in", "Joe has a balance of £42" [AE].

**When.** `When` steps describe an event or an action: "This can be a person interacting with the system, or it can be an event triggered by another system." [V] The examples: "Guess a word", "Invite a friend", "Withdraw money" [AE] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "When"). The "Imagine it's 1922" admonition appears here in a longer form: examples should make no assumptions about "technology or user interface" [V], and "Implementation details should be hidden in the step definitions." [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "When").

**Then.** `Then` steps describe an expected outcome or result [AP]. The step definition of a `Then` step should use an assertion to compare the actual outcome (what the system actually does) with the expected outcome (what the step says it should do) [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then"). An outcome should be on an observable output, something that comes out of the system (a report, user interface or message), "and not a behaviour deeply buried inside the system (like a record in a database)" [V]. The examples: "See that the guessed word was wrong", "Receive an invitation", "Card should be swallowed" [AE]. On checking the database in `Then` steps, the page says "resist that temptation!" [V]: "You should only verify an outcome that is observable for the user (or external system), and changes to a database are usually not." [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then").

**And, But.** Successive `Given` or `Then` steps can be written with the same keyword repeated, or replaced with `And` and `But` for a more fluid structure; the page shows the same "Multiple Givens" example both ways [AE] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "And, But").

**`*`.** An asterisk can replace any normal step keyword, which helps when steps are effectively a list of things, so they read like bullet points where `And` might not read so elegantly [AP]. The example is a shopping scenario listing eggs, milk and butter [AE] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "\*").

#### Background

When the same `Given` steps recur in every scenario of a `Feature`, the page reads this as a sign that those steps are not essential to describing the scenarios but are "incidental details" [V], and they can be moved under a `Background` section [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Background"). A `Background` adds context to the scenarios after it; it holds one or more `Given` steps, run before each scenario but after any Before hooks (the hooks link points outside this subset) [AP]. It sits before the first `Scenario`/`Example`, at the same indentation [AP].

The first example, "Multiple site support", sets up a global administrator "Greg", a customer "Dr. Bill" and two blogs in the background, then has three scenarios about who may post where [AE]. `Background` is also supported at the `Rule` level, shown with an "Overdue tasks" feature [AE]. Only one set of `Background` steps is allowed per `Feature` or `Rule`; scenarios that need different backgrounds should be split into more `Rule`s or `Feature`s [AP]. Conditional hooks are named as a less explicit alternative (the link points outside this subset) [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Background").

**Tips for using Background** (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Tips for using Background"):

- Don't use `Background` to set up complicated states unless the client actually needs to know that state; if user and site names don't matter to the client, use a higher-level step such as `Given I am logged in as a site owner` [AP].
- Keep the `Background` short, because the client must remember it while reading the scenarios; if it runs past 4 lines, consider moving irrelevant details into higher-level steps [AP].
- Make the `Background` vivid, with colourful names and a story; the page says the human brain keeps track of stories much better than names like "User A", "User B" or "Site 1" [AP].
- Keep scenarios short, and don't have too many; once the `Background` has scrolled off the screen, the reader loses the overview, so think about higher-level steps or splitting the `*.feature` file [AP].

#### Scenario Outline

`Scenario Outline` runs the same `Scenario` several times with different combinations of values; `Scenario Template` is a synonym [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Scenario Outline"). "Copying and pasting scenarios to use different values quickly becomes tedious and repetitive" [V]; the page collapses two cucumber-eating scenarios (12 minus 5 leaves 7; 20 minus 5 leaves 15) into one outline with `<start>`, `<eat>` and `<left>` parameters and an `Examples` table [AE].

#### Examples (the keyword)

A `Scenario Outline` must contain one or more `Examples` (or `Scenarios`) sections [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Examples"). Its steps are a template that is never run directly; the outline runs once for each row of the `Examples` table beneath it, not counting the header row [AP]. Steps refer to the table's headers through `<>`-delimited parameters, which Cucumber replaces with the row's values before it matches the step to a step definition [AP]. Parameters can also appear in the outline's description and in multiline step arguments [AP].

### Step Arguments

When a step needs more data than fits on one line, Gherkin offers `Doc Strings` and `Data Tables` [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Step Arguments").

#### Doc Strings

Doc Strings pass a larger piece of text to a step definition, set between delimiter lines of three double-quote marks; the example is a blog post with a Markdown body [AE] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Doc Strings"). The step definition need not match the text in its pattern; the text is passed automatically as the last argument [AP]. The indentation of the opening `"""` does not matter (common practice is two spaces in from the step), but "The indentation inside the triple quotes, however, is significant." [V] Each line is dedented according to the opening `"""`, so indentation beyond that column is preserved [AP].

Three backticks also work as the delimiter, which the page says may be familiar to people used to Markdown [AP]. A warning notes: "Whilst all current versions of Cucumber support backticks as the delimiter, many tools like text editors don't (yet)." [V] A Doc String can be annotated with its content type after the opening delimiter (for example `"""markdown`) [AE], under a parallel warning that many tools such as text editors do not yet support this [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Doc Strings").

#### Data Tables

Data Tables pass a list of values to a step definition; the example lists users with name, email and twitter columns [AE]. Like Doc Strings, a table is passed as the step definition's last argument [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Data Tables"). In a cell, a newline is written `\n`, a pipe is escaped `\|`, and a backslash is escaped `\\` [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Table Cell Escaping"). Cucumber provides a rich API for manipulating tables from step definitions, with the reference linked on GitHub under cucumber-jvm (outside this subset) [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Data Table API").

### Spoken Languages

The language chosen for Gherkin should be the one the users and domain experts use when they talk about the domain, and translating between two languages should be avoided [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Spoken Languages"). That is why Gherkin has been translated into "over 70 languages" [V]. The page shows a Norwegian feature, "Gjett et ord", with two examples, "Ordmaker starter et spill" and "Gjetter blir med" [AE]. A `# language:` header on a feature file's first line sets the spoken language (for example `# language: fr` for French); without it, Cucumber defaults to English (`en`) [AP]. Some Cucumber implementations also let the default language be set in configuration [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Spoken Languages").

### Step organization

Step definitions can live in one file or many. A project will probably start with them in one file; as it grows, the page says to split them into meaningful groups in different files, which makes the project more logical and easier to maintain [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Step organization").

**How Cucumber finds your features and step definitions.** Whatever the directory structure, Cucumber effectively flattens the `features/` directory tree when running tests [AP]. Anything ending in the language's step-definition file extension (the tape carries an unrendered `<Term>file-extension</Term>` placeholder here) inside the directory where Cucumber runs is treated as a step definition, and in the same directory Cucumber searches for a `Feature` corresponding to that step definition; this is the default case or the location given with the relevant option [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "How Cucumber finds your features and step definitions").

**Grouping step definitions.** "Technically it doesn't matter how you name your step definition files, or which step definitions you put in a file." [V] One giant file is possible but becomes messy and hard to maintain as the project grows; the page recommends a separate steps file for each domain concept, with one file per major domain object as a rule of thumb (both terms are unrendered `<Term>` placeholders in the tape) [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Grouping step definitions"). Its example, a Curriculum Vitae application, has Employee, Education, Experience and Authentication step-definition files, shown with file names for Java, Kotlin, Ruby, JavaScript and Go; the first three hold the `Given`, `When` and `Then` steps for creating, reading, updating and deleting those kinds of objects, and the last holds steps for logging in and out and what a given user may do [AE]. Following this pattern avoids the "Feature-coupled step definitions" anti-pattern, linked to a guide outside this subset [AP]. How steps are grouped is left to the team, so long as the grouping is meaningful to its project [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Grouping step definitions").

**Writing step definitions.** "Don't write step definitions for steps that are not present in one of your scenarios." [V] Unused ones may become cruft to clean up later; implement only what is needed, since the code can always be refactored as the project grows [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Writing step definitions").

**Avoid duplication.** Similar step definitions lead to clutter; documenting steps helps, but abstracting them with helper methods "can do wonders" [V] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Avoid duplication"). The example: `Given I go to the home page`, `Given I check the about page of the website` and `Given I get the contact details`, if each opens a web page, may be redundant steps whose behaviour is essentially the same, so they can be reduced to one step, `Given I go to the {} page` [AE]. The page shows the matching step definition in Java, Kotlin, JavaScript and Ruby as a `"I go to the {string} page"` expression, and in Go as a regular expression, each calling a page-opening helper [AE]. "Your step definitions are the glue to the actual code" [V], and they can hide implementation details by calling several reusable helper methods from one step definition [AP]. The page lists the gains as increased maintainability, increased scalability with reusable steps, and more understandable tests, and says other behaviours, such as validating a web page or clicking a button, can be handled the same way; using Data Tables for step inputs also helps maintainability and understandability [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Avoid duplication").

**Helper methods.** "Always keep in mind that Cucumber is a DSL wrapper around the programming language whose full expressiveness remains available to you in the step definition files" [V], but not in feature files [AP]. On the other hand, every step called as such in a step definition file is first parsed by Gherkin and must follow the same syntax as feature files [AP]. Refactoring step definitions into helper methods is recommended for modularity and reuse; the method can sit in the same file as the step definition, and this makes the project more understandable for later joiners and easier to maintain [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Helper methods").

### Localisation

Gherkin's keywords have been translated into many languages so that Gherkin can be written in them, and "To improve readability and flow, some languages may have more than one translation for any given keyword." [V] All translations are on GitHub, which is also where translations are added or updated [AP] (docs/gherkin/languages.mdx, "Localisation"). The page says a list of the currently supported languages and their keywords follows; in the tape that list is a bare `<GherkinLanguages/>` component tag, so the languages and their keywords are not in this reference (docs/gherkin/languages.mdx, "Localisation").

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Picking BDD's practices in any order.* Framed as a myth: discovery must come before formulation, and formulation before automation (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can pick and choose the practices in any order").
- *Automating scenarios after the code is written, and calling it BDD.* Framed as a myth: the page calls it "a perfectly reasonable way to do test automation" while denying it is BDD (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can automate scenarios after the code is implemented").
- *Discovery done by one person.* Framed as a myth and "not BDD"; discovery must be collaborative (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Discovery doesn't need a conversation").
- *Using Cucumber as proof of doing BDD.* Framed as a myth, echoing the landing page's "much more to BDD than just using Cucumber" (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Using Cucumber means you're doing BDD"; docs/bdd/index.md, "Behaviour-Driven Development").
- *BDD as a replacement for an agile process.* The landing page says BDD does not replace it but enhances it (docs/bdd/index.md, "BDD and agile").
- *Procedural, imperative scenarios.* The page sets the declarative style against step-by-step UI procedures ("procedural reference"), while granting that imperative tests "communicate details" and suit some contexts (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour"; "Consider a more declarative style").
- *`Then` steps that check the database.* The reference tells readers to resist the temptation and verify only observable outcomes (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then").
- *Feature-coupled step definitions.* Named as an anti-pattern that grouping step definitions by domain concept avoids; the anti-pattern's own page is outside this subset (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Grouping step definitions").

All 12 pages in the tape were read in full, every line (1,210 lines). The rest of the site, including installation, the language-specific guides and the blog, is not taken. This reference records those links and nothing of their content.

Per the manifest, front matter was dropped from ten pages and MDX import lines from two (`docs/gherkin/index.mdx`, `docs/gherkin/languages.mdx`), nothing was dropped from `docs/bdd/index.md`, and the text is otherwise byte for byte. Headings are cited as the tape spells them, including Markdown emphasis in the three practice headings.
